Bartender knowledge expectation:

Hey all! Traffic and content has been limited recently due to the limitations on Voat, (the invite-only feature, specifically) however, I wanted to share an experience of mine, and go over some of the basics of what your bartender should be familiar with.

I ventured out with a friend of mine to a popular bar in the downtown Phoenix area of AZ. This is one of those establishments that is high volume, and fast paced! (If you want specifics, just message me) They have several rails (bar tops,) and many different bartenders. However, fast paced does not need to mean poor quality!

My first drink of the evening was fairly standard for me, a Trash Can - this drink includes all the basics of a Long Island Iced Tea, (Vodka, Gin, Rum, Tequila, Triple Sec, Sour, Coke) excluding the Coke for Blue Curacao, and a Red Bull. The front-end bartender had no idea where to start! I should state that this is a very popular drink in this part of the country. Needless to say, I was disappointed.

I've decided to give you guys an idea of what it's reasonable to expect from your bartender...

  1. Call Drink (Single Liquor + Mixer) - 10 seconds
  2. Beer & Wine (Pour and go) - 5-10 seconds max
  3. Basic Cocktails (Martinis, Margaritas, Mojitos, and others that don't happen to start with M) 15-30 seconds.
  4. Standard Shots (Washington Apple, Jager Bomb, Red-Headed Slut, etc.) - 10-20 seconds.

My second experience with a bartender this evening was a relief! A Washington Apple shot was in front of me after 10 seconds with very little thought or delay required by the bartender. He was also engaging, and kind! Rest assured, my tip reflected both his knowledge, efficiency, and overall service!.

I feel that it's safe for any one of you to go out to a bar and expect your bartender to have a few key things in their repertoire:

  1. Drink Knowledge
  2. Courtesy
  3. Efficiency
  4. Respect
  5. Confidence

It doesn't take a whole lot more than this to give your bar guests an experience they'll want to return for!

Don't get me wrong, boys and girls, not all bartenders are the same; and some are more knowledgeable than others. Personally, I feel that confidence is one of the more appealing qualities a bartender can possess. @redwood may give me a hard time here, but I think that a bartender who confidently makes a drink wrong, is better than a bartender who fumbles through the process of making a fairly standard drink correctly. This, is frankly, a purely psychological reaction to actually watching them make your drink. If it looks like they didn't know what the hell they were doing, it's probably just not going to taste very good. I acknowledge that this might not be everyone's experience.

I'm somewhat grumpy as I'm writing this post, because I'm a few drinks in this evening, and also because I had to re-write this entire post due to technical difficulties. (I know there was such better formatting and content to the post I lost!)

Feel free to share your thoughts, criticisms, differences of opinion, or just personal stories! I want to keep dialogue moving on this sub, and I hope that you guys will help me out.

Adieu,

What should you expect from your Bartender?
This can be considered an elaboration on a response to this post queried by @MrHarryReems.
How much time is given to a new/aspiring bartender to get on the level described?

Perfectly valid question, but one that's hard to answer because of the various ways people achieve the position. My recommendation for people wanting to start out behind the bar is to work their way up from Serving, Bar backing, or some other entry level position with an establishment; this gives the individual an opportunity to learn from the ground up, and if the establishment is worth a damn, there's someone there who'll take an aspiring bartender under their wing - and get them moving in the right direction. To try and summarize an answer for your question... I'd say that someone who is promoted to a Bartender, (after going through the process of learning the ropes as a bar back) should be able to confidently pour drinks, and know their craft within a few months. There are so many variables to how one learns the trade, however, that I can't narrow it down much more than that. Thanks for your question!
Thanks for your answer, I learned something today.

A trash can isn't popular in my part of the country, but I know the recipe because a friend of mine would drink them with me on St. Patrick's day, a tradition starting when we were about 16 or so. We know it as an "Irish Trash Can," but that's beside the point.

I've always felt that knowledge is important, but the ability to ask is even more important. Not only that, but a lot of expectations change for quite a few reasons. I've been asked to make all kinds of crazy shit. I've been asked to make a drink called "satan's amnesty," which turned out to be something a college student made up in his house, yet he expected that I know it. I've also been asked to make "this" as the customer points to a picture of a cocktail on pinterest. Have you ever been asked for a purple cooter shooter? or a golden cadillac? or a democrat? Those are 3 different types of obscure drinks, one is regional, one is from a faded era with strange ingredients, and one is a great classic that is right on the verge of a comeback. There are a metric fuck ton of drinks, and you can't learn them all.

You should know the popular cocktails, shooters, and the basic formulas that make those drinks. You should have the conversational skills to know how to ask when you don't know.

But there's something to consider here. If it's any normal day, I will talk with a customer, and figure it out with them. If it is the one night of the week that we get hit harder than any other place in town, where every single person is waiting patiently for a drink, and you rudely ask for an inverted swedish hand-job, and you don't know what's in it, what the hell were you expecting?

The responsibility of the bartender is not only to make sure you have the drink you want, but also the experience you want. Sometimes one precludes the other. If I can't make you're drink, but we figure something out together, we're going to have a good time. If I can't make you're drink, and you take it personally and offensively, I will step two inches to the right to ask one of the other 2k people in the bar what they'd like.

This example isn't directed at you as it's extreme, and an irish trash can isn't obscure, but I just wanted to add some contrast. I'd also like to say that there are plenty of places that hire bartenders and don't train them, and that is inexcuseable.
